title: If Only I Knew Where to Find Him
summary: Job ignores Eliphaz's accusations and speaks of his longing to find God and lay his case before him, confident that an upright man would be heard. But God is nowhere to be found, east, west, north, or south. Job trusts that God knows his way and that testing will prove him gold, yet he is terrified by a God who does whatever he wills.
story: Eliphaz has just accused Job of cruelty to the poor and urged him to return to God (chapter 22). Job's reply (chapters 23 and 24) does not answer the charges point by point. Instead he turns from the friends to God, as he did in chapters 9, 13, and 19. The legal hope that grew through those chapters, the wish for a hearing before God, comes back here in its most personal form: Job's problem is not only that God seems unjust but that God is absent. This chapter moves between confidence and dread more quickly than any before it. The longing for a hearing will reach its climax in chapter 31, where Job signs his defense and calls on the Almighty to answer. God will answer, though not in the way Job imagines, from the whirlwind in chapter 38.
historical:
The chapter's world is the undated patriarchal setting of Uz. Its imagery draws on legal procedure familiar across the ancient Near East. A plaintiff who wanted justice would go to the place where the king or judge sat, set his case in order, and present his arguments (verses 3-4). The word translated seat in verse 3 refers to a fixed place or dwelling, and Job pictures God's throne as a courtroom where a hearing might be had, if only he knew how to get there.

The directions in verses 8-9 reflect the way Hebrew described the compass. A person oriented himself by facing east, toward the sunrise, so the word for east also means in front, west means behind, north is literally the left hand, and south the right hand. Job has looked in front of him, behind him, to his left, and to his right, and God is nowhere.
cultural:
The metal imagery of verse 10 comes from the smelting and refining of gold, well known in the ancient world. Ore was heated in a crucible until the impurities separated and the pure metal remained. The image is common in the Old Testament for God's testing of his people (Psalm 66:10, Zechariah 13:9, Malachi 3:3). Job uses it in a surprising way. The friends assume that suffering exposes hidden sin. Job believes that his testing will prove him pure, not reveal him as dross.

Verses 11-12 use the language of walking a path, a common ancient picture of moral life: to keep God's way without turning aside, to follow in his tracks. Job also speaks of treasuring the words of God's mouth more than his daily bread. Bread was the staple food of the ancient world, and to treasure something more than daily bread was to value it above survival itself.
literary: The chapter falls into three movements, each marked by a change of mood. In verses 2-7 Job imagines finding God and presenting his case; the tone is wistful and even hopeful, and he pictures God listening rather than overpowering him (verse 6). In verses 8-12 hope meets reality: God cannot be found in any direction, but Job is confident that God knows his way, and he defends his faithfulness. In verses 13-17 confidence gives way to fear, because the God who knows Job's innocence is also unchangeable and does what he desires. The line “He is unchangeable” in verse 13 translates a compact Hebrew phrase that literally reads something like he is in one, and some translators render it he is one or he has decided. Verse 17 is also difficult; the BSB reads it as a statement of resolve, while other translations make it a wish that Job had vanished in the darkness. The chapter ends not with resolution but with the image of thick darkness covering Job's face.

outline.t: If only I could find God and present my case
God is hidden, but he knows my way
Terror before the God who does as he pleases

doctrines.note: Job confesses that God does what he desires and no one can turn him back (verse 13). For Job this is not comfort but terror, since he cannot see God's purpose. The chapter shows that the doctrine of God's sovereignty, true as it is, can be a heavy thing to hold in suffering.

Job interprets his suffering as a test rather than a punishment (verse 10). He has not been told about the scene in heaven (chapters 1 and 2), yet he reaches a truth the reader already knows: God is not destroying him for sin.

The chapter is a portrait of the hiddenness of God. Job looks everywhere and cannot find him. Scripture is honest that believers experience God as absent, and the book will answer Job's longing only when God himself chooses to speak.

words.note: Bachan, to test or examine. It is used of assaying metals and, figuratively, of God testing hearts and minds. In verse 10 Job says that when God has tested him, he will come forth as gold. The word assumes a process with a purpose and an outcome.

Mishpat, justice, judgment, or a legal case. In verse 4 it refers to Job's case, the formal argument he would present. The word is central to the book, which asks whether God's governing of the world is just and whether a human being can obtain justice from him.

Tsaphan, to hide, store up, or treasure. Job says he has treasured the words of God's mouth (verse 12). The same verb appears in Psalm 119:11 for storing God's word in the heart. Job's claim is not only that he avoided sin but that he loved God's words.

Ophel, deep darkness or gloom. It is a poetic word, used for the darkness of night and for the gloom of distress. In verse 17 it is the thick darkness that covers Job's face, the last image of the chapter.

christ: Job's cry to find God and stand before his seat is a longing the New Testament presents as answered in Christ. John's Gospel says that no one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son has made him known (John 1:18), and Hebrews invites believers to draw near to the throne of grace with confidence because Jesus is a high priest who sympathizes with human weakness (Hebrews 4:14-16). The link is thematic: Job does not predict a mediator here, though he has longed for one before (9:33, 16:19-21). Jesus also knew God's hiddenness. On the cross he cried out in the words of Psalm 22, asking why God had forsaken him (Mark 15:34). The gospel does not remove Job's experience of darkness; it shows the Son of God entering it.

hard.q: Job says God cannot be found anywhere. How does that square with the belief that God is everywhere?
hard.a: The Old Testament teaches that God is present everywhere (Psalm 139 says there is no place one can flee from his presence). Job does not deny this; in the same chapter he says God knows the way he has taken (verse 10). What he describes is the experience of God's hiddenness: God is present but silent, near but not accessible for the hearing Job wants. Many interpreters distinguish between God's presence everywhere and his favorable, revealing presence, the kind experienced in worship or answered prayer. The Psalms often lament the hiding of God's face (Psalms 13 and 88, for example). Others emphasize that Job's words are honest poetry of distress, not a doctrine of God, and that the book allows him to speak this way without rebuke. Both readings agree that Scripture takes the experience of God's absence seriously, and that the right response is not to deny it but to bring it to God, as Job does.

questions: Job says, “If only I knew where to find Him.” When have you felt that God was hidden, and what did you do with that feeling?
Job believes that testing will prove him gold rather than expose him as dross. How can someone tell the difference between God's refining and God's judgment?
Job treasures God's words more than his daily bread, yet he is terrified of God. How can love and fear of God exist together?
